RNNs look really cool, am I wrong in assuming that their power is in their ability to analyze non-sequential data (such as an image)? This is what I gathered from that (excellent) link you provided. My understanding is that input to RNNs is converted to a vector, as with most complex nets. They receive input images the same way as any other input data, usually a big list of (essentially) unstructured activation signals.

The real strength of RNNs is more that they have a degree of "memory" and are able to detect and respond to higher order patterns. I think the article I linked mentioned a net trained on a bunch of Wikipedia text, which was able to learn that xml <tag>s should always have exactly one matching end </tag>, no matter what was between them. In that case, the input layer may never have been presented both a start and an end tag at the same time (the net never "saw" both parts at once), but it was still able to figure out the connection.

I'd guess the right choice depends more on what you want to use the network for. If you're just trying to classify or detect fairly simple "instantaneous" patterns, "traditional" networks can be trained to be pretty effective. If you're more looking to do higher level pattern recognition, anything that depends on "context" (and you've got a pile of spare horsepower) RNNs seem to be the hot topic right now.

Honestly though, I don't know nearly enough to recommend anything to you, since I'm barely more than a layman in this field.

Popular fast-rising posts from any sub are on /v/all, while popular fast-rising posts from subs you subscribe to are on your front page.
